Scoring the vulnerability finding against the provided packet evidence and rubric.

The finding involves memory poisoning through an unconfined write_file tool. An attacker can overwrite the memory file with a forged entry that carries a copy-to-attacker rule. The unsigned memory file allows the forged entry to load as valid.

The attack path starts with a write_file tool call targeting the memory file. The S2 path flaw makes this reachable. In a later session the system prompt presents the entry as trusted instructions. The model copies outgoing email to the attacker.

The agent is a CLI, not a public endpoint. The attacker is a user of the CLI who triggers the write_file call. The path_id is asl/s8/write-file/memory-file-tamper/next-session/send-email-copy.

The attack path is now fully mapped: a request triggers the model to call write_file on the memory file with a forged entry. The unsigned file allows the entry to load as valid. In a later session the system prompt presents it as trusted instructions. The model then copies outgoing email to the attacker.

The vulnerable system is the agent application. The attacker must get the model to write to the memory file. Because the agent is a CLI with no network listener, the attacker likely needs local access or must inject content that causes the model to write the file.

The source citation is s8-memory-poisoning.md:13. The attack vector is AV:N because the agent is a local CLI with no public endpoint. A local user could trigger the write_file call directly. Fetch_url could also bring in attacker content that causes the model to write the memory file.

This finding is distinct from ASL-S8a. It relies on write_file to overwrite the memory file directly, not on the remember tool. The lab places the memory path in the workspace. The default memory file location is referenced in config.py:15.

The write_file tool joins paths to the workspace without containment. Absolute paths, dot-dot sequences, and symlinks can escape workspace boundaries. This means the memory file could reside outside the workspace yet remain reachable via path traversal. The default configuration placement is therefore less relevant to the vulnerability.

The agent has no authentication. A local user can trigger the write_file call directly.

The attack vector is AV:L. The agent is a local CLI with no network listener. The attacker must be a local user who invokes the CLI directly. The compose lab network is internal.

The proof of concept uses a scripted MockModel rather than a real model. Because the lab never ran real model exploits for S1 and S3, the reliability of this path is uncertain. Attack complexity is therefore likely Medium, since a real model must be convinced to issue the write_file call.

Model compliance is treated as attack complexity in agent vulnerability scoring. The CVSS v4.0 base vector requires exactly eleven base metrics: AV, AC, AT, PR, UI, VC, VI, VA, SC, SI, and SA. The attack requirements metric is new in v4.0.

The attack requirements metric is None. The unconfined write_file tool makes the memory file reachable by default, so no deployment-specific condition is required.

Privileges Required is being weighed between None and Low. The agent is a local CLI with no authentication, so a normal user can invoke it. The attacker may be the same person running the application, which would make the requirement None. Alternatively, local user access might be necessary, which would make it Low.

Privileges Required is Low. A local user must be able to invoke the agent, which is a basic user capability. The attack vector is Local.

The threat model is being reconsidered. The attacker might be the legitimate user of the agent, or injected content might trigger the write_file call. This is the file-tamper route of memory poisoning, distinct from the remember tool route.
